name: Hashable
first: A protocol for a type whose values can be compared for equality and turned into one integer, their hash value, so that they can be the members of a set or the keys of a dictionary.

dependsOn.why: Hashable is a protocol, whose requirements are the comparison and the hash.
dependsOn.whyInExample: The type `City` conforms to `Hashable`, as `Friendly` conforms to `Greeter`.

dependsOn.why: swiftc writes the comparison and the hash for a structure from its stored properties.
dependsOn.whyInExample: The type `City` is a structure with two stored properties, `name` and `country`, as `Trip` has `city` and `nights` on the page of Structure.

sil.shows: swiftc writes the comparison of two cities for City, which compares country as well as name.
swiftc writes the method hash(into:) for City, which gives name to the hasher.
The method hash(into:) gives country to the hasher too, so the hash value comes from both properties.

what.is: A type that conforms to the protocol `Hashable` has values that can be compared for equality, with `==`, and hashed: turned into one integer, the hash value, which is the same for every two equal values. A set and a dictionary find a value by its hash value, so their members and keys must be hashable.
what.afterExample: The constants `lima` and `again` are two instances with the same values, so they are equal. The set on line 9 keeps only one of them, and the dictionary on line 11 finds the value for `lima` when it is given `again`.
what.problem: A set must know when two values are the same, so that it keeps one, and a dictionary must find a key's value without comparing the key with every key it has. A hash value tells them where to look, so they compare only the few values kept there.
what.how: When every stored property of a structure is hashable, swiftc writes `==` and the hash for it. The comparison `==` compares each property, and the hash combines the hash of each property. Two equal values give the same hash value, so a set or a dictionary finds equal values in the same place.

when.text: Use it for a type whose values are members of a set or keys of a dictionary, such as a city, or that tell the items of a list apart.
Don't write `==` and the hash yourself when swiftc can write them. Written by hand, two equal values must still give the same hash value, or a set or a dictionary can lose them.

parts.name: The conformance to `Hashable`, line 1
parts.text: The colon and the name `Hashable` after `City` say that `City` conforms to the protocol `Hashable`. Its stored properties, `name` and `country`, are strings, which are hashable, so swiftc writes the comparison and the hash for `City`.

parts.name: The equal-to operator, line 8
parts.text: Two equal signs compare two values, and give true when they are equal. The `==` that swiftc writes for `City` gives true when `name` and `country` are both equal.

parts.name: The hash values, lines 9 and 11
parts.text: A set and a dictionary hash each value they are given: they turn it into one integer, from the hash of each stored property. Equal values give the same integer, so `again` is found where `lima` was put.

steps.text: Lines 6 and 7 make two cities with the same name and the same country.
Line 8 compares them with `==`, which compares `name` and then `country`. Both are equal, so it prints {{true}}.
Line 9 makes a set of `lima` and `again`. The set hashes each one. They give the same hash value and are equal, so the set keeps only one.
Line 10 prints how many members the set has: {{1}}.
Line 11 makes a dictionary with `lima` as its one key, for the value 4.

Line 12 looks up `again`. Its hash value is the hash value of `lima`, and the two are equal, so the dictionary finds 4, and line 12 prints {{4}}. With no such key, it would give 0, the value after `default:`.

end.text: Equal cities gave the same hash value, so the set kept one of them, and the dictionary found the value of `lima` from `again`.
